catalog_quote: Current data provides evidence for two lexically contrastive tonemes, a high level tone, which is marked with an acute accent á, and a low level tone, which is marked with a grave accent à. The tone-bearing unit in Kufo appears to be the syllable. ... It is worth noting that tone contrasts have not yet been observed in monosyllabic words, which all appear to carry a high tone when elicited within a frame without a following long pause, and which carry a falling tone otherwise. Tonal minimal pairs are rare, and tone appears to have a low functional load both lexically and grammatically based on the data collected for the current project. ... [p.116] Kufo tone appears to be an inseparable component of the stems and is not altered during verb conjugations and noun singularisation or pluralisation. In future work, pitch conditioning and intonation will be particularly worth studying. ... In…

new_statements.quote: The tone system has not been fully analysed for any of the Kadugli-Krongo languages. Reh (1983) establishes High and Low tone for Krongo-Tabanya and states that it is significant both lexically and grammatically. [...] The other Kadugli-Krongo languages that we have studied also have two tones, with a considerable amount of pitch conditioning. A few words in Kamda and in Kadugli seem to have a mid pitch also. In all of the languages there are only a limited number of lexical contrasts based on tone (example 23). Tone probably carries a greater grammatical functional load.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has an empty rule for Kufo; this is the first primary-source suprasegmental statement: tonal, no word-stress statement. Covers the whole Kadugli-Krongo group (Keiga, Kamda, Kadugli, Miri, Katcha, Kanga, Kufa, Krongo) from the authors' own fieldwork, with Kufa examples.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kufo (called Kufa here) and the other Kadugli-Krongo languages have a two-tone (High/Low) system with heavy pitch conditioning, few lexical tone contrasts and a mainly grammatical function of tone. The article has no stress section and makes no statement about word stress; its only mention of stress is an orthographic remark (p. 62) that the letter <x> was chosen to leave room for diacritics 'if these were needed for features such as tone or stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the authors say the tone system is not fully analysed for any Kadugli-Krongo language
new_statements.identity_note: Hall & Hall 2004 call the language 'Kufa' and describe the whole Kadugli-Krongo group (Keiga, Kamda, Kadugli, Miri, Katcha, Kanga, Kufa, Krongo) together, with a Kufa minimal pair; Mullan 2022 describes Kufo from 2021 fieldwork with a Khartoum-based speaker (KCP1) and notes Kufo is closely related to Kanga. Blench 2004 equates Kufo with Kufa.

new_statements.quote: Kufo is a tonal language with both lexical and grammatical tone. Kufo has two tones, high and low, which are borne by the syllable. High tones are represented with an acute accent and low tones are unmarked. [...] Tone is generally considered to have a larger grammatical than lexical function in Kadu languages (Hall & Hall, 2004, p. 7). This holds true in Kufo, where the main function of tone seems to be distinguishing forms of the verb rather than distinguishing between lexemes.

new_statements.quote: All Kadu languages are almost certainly tone languages. I have more or less uncritically assumed a two tone system, and I have occasionally heard and marked downstep. Falling tones are rare, and rising tones even more so. Reh, too, describes Krongo and Yegang as having two-tone Systems, and she points out cases where tone distinguishes lexical items as well as different grammatical forms of the same item. Matsushita (1984) found that Talla had a three-tone system, though his mid tone seems to be less common than either high or low tone. The tonal variations, both within and across languages, are indicative of interesting tonal processes, but the data are insufficient to analyse thé various tonal Systems. [p. 19:] High tone is marked with an acute accent; low tone is unmarked.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kufo has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. The work adds that Kufo, like all Kadu languages, is (tentatively) a two-tone language and is silent on stress; it supplies no stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Schadeberg treats all nine Kadu languages, Kufo (his no. 3, Stevenson's 'Kanga', ~100-item list) included, as tone languages, transcribed with an assumed two-tone (H vs L) system plus occasional downstep; falling tones rare, rising rarer. The paper contains no statement of any kind about word stress, accent placement or prominence; the words 'stress' and 'accent' (other than 'acute accent' as a tone diacritic) do not occur.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning prosody. The tone claim is explicitly tentative ('almost certainly', 'more or less uncritically assumed a two tone system') and family-wide rather than Kufo-specific; Talla is reported (after Matsushita 1984) with three tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Schadeberg's Kufo data are his language no. 3 'Kufo: Stevenson "Kanga", dialect of Kufa' (locality kuufo), about 100 items elicited 1974-75 from one speaker, Jakeliin Faddala (b. 1958 at Kassala, learned Kufo from her grandmother, resident at Kufo since 1972). The tone statement quoted is a generalization over all nine Kadu languages surveyed, not a Kufo-specific analysis.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at pp.104 and 116 of the Li 2022 PDF we hold; 'stress' never occurs in the thesis. (2) The deciding source is a 2022 phonology thesis with acoustic tone data, the only phonology of this languoid; Glottolog's two descriptive refs are a morphology thesis and field notes. (3) I downloaded all three reachable non-held descriptions (Hall & Hall 2004 OPSL 9 p.65; Mullan 2022 pp.15-16; Blench 2004 Ogmios): the first two independently state a two-tone (H/L, syllable TBU) system with lexical and grammatical function and say nothing about word stress; the third is silent. Nothing found suggests a stress/accent analysis exists for Kufo or any Kanga variety, so tonal with domain not stated by the source stands. tone.quote: The CVCV words also included consonants of a range of places and manners of articulation, and had a range of tonal patterns. ... The present study aids preparation for future studies on tonal patterns in the Kufo language. Though the Kadu languages are often hypothesised as tonal, their tone systems have never been systematically studied. The findings on contrastive vowel quality and length allow these characteristics to be controlled for in analyses focusing on tone, in order for the prosodic system of Kufo to be better understood.
